phonemes.desc: Sigma plus short epsilon — the name begins softly, like moonlight.
Lambda plus acute on short epsilon — the pitched peak, bright but cool.
Long eta — the final vowel that sustains like a nocturnal note.

pronunciation.approximation: 'seh-LAY-nay' — the second syllable carries the pitch, and the final vowel is long and pale.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *seh₂l- 'shine' — root of Greek σελήνη, Latin luna, English 'shine'

kin.label: Lunar
kin.form: Selene is the moon personified; her Roman equivalent is Luna

pronunciation.note: Selḗnē is Tier 1 because the Greek Σελήνη contains both stress (acute on the short έ) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name shares a root with 'shine' and 'lunar' across Indo-European languages.

domains.title: The Moon
domains.subtitle: Night, Cycles, Magic, and Sleep
domains.lead: Selḗnē is the moon personified: a goddess who drives her silver chariot through the night, governs the menstrual cycle, and presides over dreams and magic. Where Hēlios reveals, Selḗnē conceals and transforms.

cards.name: The Silver Chariot
cards.desc: She crosses the night sky in a chariot drawn by oxen or horses, the counterpart to Hēlios's golden car.

cards.name: Cycles and Time
cards.desc: The month is hers; she governs menstruation, tides, planting, and ritual calendars.

cards.name: Dreams and Magic
cards.desc: Hecate's ally; witches draw down the moon to work spells and send dreams.

cards.name: The Lover
cards.desc: She fell in love with the shepherd Endymion and put him to eternal sleep so he would not age.

symbols.name: Crescent moon
symbols.meaning: Her boat or bow; the waxing and waning phases

symbols.name: Oxen
symbols.meaning: The animals that draw her chariot

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: The pale light she carries through darkness

symbols.name: Veil
symbols.meaning: The clouds that obscure and reveal her

mythology.lead: Selḗnē's myths are fewer than Hēlios's because the night was less personified in Greek poetry. Her most famous story is a love affair with a mortal.

myths.title: Endymion on Mount Latmus
myths.text: Selḗnē fell in love with Endymion, a beautiful shepherd or king, and asked Zeús to grant him eternal youth. Zeüs put him into eternal sleep in a cave on Mount Latmus in Caria. Each night Selḗnē visits him; some say their union produced fifty daughters. The myth turns the moon's monthly return into a romantic rendezvous and makes sleep the price of immortality.

myths.title: The Moon's Journey
myths.text: Like Hēlios, Selḗnē drives a chariot across the sky. The Homeric Hymn to Selene (1–7) describes her as 'winged' and 'golden-crowned,' driving her chariot through the night while Hēlios rests. The moon's pale light is her garment; her crown marks her as a queen of heaven.

myths.title: The Cattle of the Moon
myths.text: Selḗnē was sometimes said to drive oxen rather than horses, connecting her to agricultural time and the lunar calendar that governed planting. The white bull or ox became a lunar symbol across the ancient Mediterranean, linking her to both fertility and sacrifice.

myths.title: Drawing Down the Moon
myths.text: In Greek magical papyri and later Neoplatonic theurgy, Selḗnē could be 'drawn down' by rituals to empower spells, especially those involving love, dreams, and transformation. The Thessalian witches of Roman literature were famous for pulling the moon from the sky. This magical Selḗnē merged with Hekátē and Artemis as a triple lunar goddess.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Selḗnē with Luna, though as with Hēlios/Sol, the Greek goddess was increasingly absorbed by Artemis-Diana in later periods. In Hellenistic and Roman Egypt, Selḗnē was syncretized with Isis, who wears a lunar disk on her head. Neoplatonists saw the moon as the boundary between the material and immaterial realms, and Selḗnē as the mediator between Hēlios and the earth. The English words 'selenography' (study of the moon's surface) and the chemical element selenium derive from her name.
lore.culturalLegacy: Selḗnē is the archetype of the moon as feminine, cyclical, and magical. She governs not only the night sky but the rhythms of women's bodies and the agricultural calendar. The crescent moon remains one of humanity's most universal symbols, appearing on flags, coins, and religious iconography across cultures. In modern witchcraft and Neopaganism, the moon goddess — whether called Selene, Diana, or Hecate — is central. Restoring Selḗnē restores the Greek name of the moon as a conscious, luminous presence.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Selḗnē is the goddess of reflected light. She does not generate radiance; she transforms what Hēlios gives. This is her power and her limitation. The night reveals what the day hides: dreams, secrets, transformations. The moon governs the liminal hours when boundaries loosen.

Modern life has banished the moon. Electric light has made her irrelevant for practical purposes, and with her disappearance has gone much of the ancient vocabulary for nocturnal experience. The restoration of her name is a small act of lunar reclamation: the night, too, has its goddess.

sources.name: Plutarch, On the Face in the Moon

lore.archaeology: Reliefs and gems from the Hellenistic and Roman periods show Selene as a winged or chariot-borne goddess with a crescent moon at her brow; the Great Altar of Pergamon includes a Luna/Selene figure. In Elis, Pausanias records a sanctuary of Selene/Sosipolis. Roman marble statues such as the 'Selene and Endymion' group (British Museum) and crescent-moon crowns on imperial coins and Isiac reliefs attest her later astral cult.
